steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a paper proposing RTFS-Net, an efficient time-frequency domain method for audio-visual speech separation. Explain the cocktail party problem, the T-domain vs TF-domain trade-off, the three shortcomings of existing TF-domain methods, and how our model and its blocks address them, plus the headline results.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Cocktail party problem; AOSS vs AVSS; T-domain vs TF-domain
- Trade-offs of T-domain and TF-domain methods
- Three reasons TF-domain methods lag behind
- RTFS-Net and our three contributions
- Experiments and results

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Background
  - 'cocktail party problem' (cite): focus on one speaker amid overlapping voices, noisy environment
  - humans effortless; machines: longstanding signal-processing challenge
  - AOSS (cite): only mixed audio; limited with strong noise, reverberation, heavy overlap
  - multi-modal: AVSS (cite), adds visual cues
  - two classes: Time-domain (T-domain) and Time-Frequency domain (TF-domain)
- T vs TF
  - T-domain (cite): long, uncompressed, high-dimensional features from 1D conv encoder (cite as proposer)
  - fine-grained, high quality, but high params/complexity -> long training, heavy GPU, slow inference
  - TF-domain (cite): complex 2D representation from STFT; large windows/hop lengths compress -> efficient
  - historically TF-domain substantially outperformed by T-domain; three critical factors
- Three factors
  - 1) amplitude/phase modelled separately in some attempts (cite), but no TF-domain AVSS models time and frequency independently/tailored
    - AOSS work (two, cite as subjects) exploited this, beat T-domain by large margins; but large LSTM (cite) and transformer (cite) -> heavy compute, unattractive for AVSS
  - 2) AVSS fusion strategies (cite) ignore visual features from multiple receptive fields; visual info = ā priōrī knowledge
  - 3) TF-domain AVSS (cite) overlook complex nature of features -> lose amplitude and phase; hurts iSTFT reconstruction
- RTFS-Net (Recursive Time-Frequency Separation Network, Figure 1)
  - novel TF-domain AVSS; computationally efficient
  - STFT audio encoder, high-fidelity pretrained video encoder, recursive RTFS Blocks for target speaker extraction
  - contributions threefold:
    - 1. RTFS Blocks: compressed subspace; model both dimensions individually then together; attention (TF-AR) restores dimensions, minimal info loss; low cost
    - 2. Cross-dimensional Attention Fusion (CAF) Block: low params, efficient, multi-head attention fuses visual cues into audio
    - 3. Spectral Source Separation (S^{3}) Block: explicitly reconstructs plural features; better separation, no extra cost
- Experiments
  - LRS2, LRS3, VoxCeleb2 (cite each)
  - first TF-domain AVSS to beat all contemporary T-domain methods
  - computational complexity -83%, parameters -90%
  - Web page with samples; code open-sourced after publication

steps.text:
The ‘cocktail party problem’ is about our ability to focus on the voice of a single speaker when there are many overlapping voices in a noisy environment. Humans solve this problem without effort, but replicating this ability in machines is still a longstanding challenge in signal-processing. Audio-only Speech Separation (AOSS) methods only use the mixed-speaker audio signal, and they have limitations when there is strong background noise, reverberation, or heavy overlap of voices. To overcome this, researchers turned to a multi-modal approach, Audio-visual Speech Separation (AVSS). AVSS methods add visual cues into the paradigm, and they can generally be split into two main classes: Time-domain (T-domain) and Time-Frequency domain (TF-domain) methods, and each one has its own benefits and challenges.

T-domain methods work on the audio features returned by the 1D convolutional encoder design that was proposed by earlier work, which are long, uncompressed and high-dimensional. This approach gives fine-grained, high quality audio separation, but the parameter count and computational complexity are high, and this leads to long training periods, intensive GPU usage and slow inference. TF-domain methods, on the other hand, apply their algorithms to the complex 2D representation that the Short-Time Fourier Transform (STFT) gives. Usually the STFT uses large windows and hop lengths to compress the data, so the separation methods are more computationally efficient. But historically, T-domain methods have substantially outperformed all TF-domain methods. From our research, this performance gap comes from three critical factors.

  - 1) amplitude/phase modelled separately in some attempts (cite), but no TF-domain AVSS models time and frequency independently/tailored

  - 3) TF-domain AVSS (cite) overlook complex nature of features -> lose amplitude and phase; hurts iSTFT reconstruction
- RTFS-Net (Recursive Time-Frequency Separation Network, Figure 1)

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
The ‘cocktail party problem’ is about our ability to focus on the voice of a single speaker when there are many overlapping voices in a noisy environment. Humans solve this problem without effort, but replicating this ability in machines is still a longstanding challenge in signal-processing. Audio-only Speech Separation (AOSS) methods only use the mixed-speaker audio signal, and they have limitations when there is strong background noise, reverberation, or heavy overlap of voices. To overcome this, researchers turned to a multi-modal approach, Audio-visual Speech Separation (AVSS). AVSS methods add visual cues into the paradigm, and they can generally be split into two main classes: Time-domain (T-domain) and Time-Frequency domain (TF-domain) methods, and each one has its own benefits and challenges.

T-domain methods work on the audio features returned by the 1D convolutional encoder design that was proposed by earlier work, which are long, uncompressed and high-dimensional. This approach gives fine-grained, high quality audio separation, but the parameter count and computational complexity are high, and this leads to long training periods, intensive GPU usage and slow inference. TF-domain methods, on the other hand, apply their algorithms to the complex 2D representation that the Short-Time Fourier Transform (STFT) gives. Usually the STFT uses large windows and hop lengths to compress the data, so the separation methods are more computationally efficient. But historically, T-domain methods have substantially outperformed all TF-domain methods. From our research, this performance gap comes from three critical factors.

First, some attempts have been made to model amplitude and phase separately, but no TF-domain AVSS method explores modelling the two acoustic dimensions (time and frequency) independently and in a tailored way, to exploit the advantage this domain has over T-domain methods. In fact, recent research in the AOSS domain by one group and another has capitalized on this advantage and outperformed the T-domain counterparts by large margins. But they use large LSTM and transformer architectures, which is a heavy computational burden, so they are not an attractive solution for AVSS. Second, existing AVSS studies have explored various strategies for audio-visual fusion, but they neglect to use visual features from multiple receptive fields to increase performance. This kind of visual information is important ā priōrī knowledge, and it is crucial for extracting the voice of the target speaker accurately. Third, TF-domain AVSS studies often overlook that the features are complex underneath, and so they lose critical amplitude and phase information when they extract the target speaker's voice from the audio mixture. This makes the reconstruction of the inverse STFT (iSTFT) worse and leads to poorer performance of the model.

In this work we propose a novel TF-domain AVSS method, the Recursive Time-Frequency Separation Network (RTFS-Net, Figure 1). It is a computationally efficient solution to the cocktail party problem, and it uses an STFT based audio encoder, a high-fidelity pretrained video encoder and a series of recursive RTFS Blocks to do target speaker extraction. We have three contributions:

- 1. Our RTFS Blocks deal with the first issue by projecting the features to a compressed subspace. In this subspace we explicitly model both acoustic dimensions individually and then in tandem, and after that we apply an attentional mechanism (TF-AR) to restore the dimensions with minimal information loss. This lets us get the benefits of independent time-frequency processing without a substantial computational cost.

- 2. Our Cross-dimensional Attention Fusion (CAF) Block is a low parameter, computationally efficient solution to the second issue. It aggregates the multi-modal information with a multi-head attention strategy so that the visual cues of the target speaker are fused optimally into the audio features, which helps high quality separation.

- 3. Our Spectral Source Separation (S^{3}) Block deals with the third issue by explicitly reconstructing the plural features of the target speaker, so separation quality is higher and computational cost does not increase.

We did comprehensive experimental evaluations on three widely used datasets, LRS2, LRS3 and VoxCeleb2, to show the value of each contribution. As far as we know, RTFS-Net is the first TF-domain AVSS method that outperforms all contemporary T-domain methods, and it does this while also having a clear advantage, reducing computational complexity by 83% and the parameter count by 90%. We also provide a Web page where sample results can be listened to, and our code will be open-sourced after publication for reproducibility.

steps.text:
The ‘cocktail party problem’ [1,2,3] is about our ability to focus on the voice of a single speaker when there are many overlapping voices in a noisy environment. Humans solve this problem without effort, but replicating this ability in machines is still a longstanding challenge in signal-processing. To overcome this, researchers turned to a multi-modal approach, Audio-visual Speech Separation (AVSS) [7,8,9]. AVSS methods add visual cues into the paradigm, and they can generally be split into two main classes: Time-domain (T-domain) and Time-Frequency domain (TF-domain) methods, and each one has its own benefits and challenges.

T-domain methods [10,9,11,12] work on the audio features returned by the 1D convolutional encoder design that was proposed by [13], which are long, uncompressed and high-dimensional. This approach gives fine-grained, high quality audio separation, but the parameter count and computational complexity are high, and this leads to long training periods, intensive GPU usage and slow inference. TF-domain methods [14,15,7], on the other hand, apply their algorithms to the complex 2D representation that the Short-Time Fourier Transform (STFT) gives. Usually the STFT uses large windows and hop lengths to compress the data, so the separation methods are more computationally efficient. But historically, T-domain methods have substantially outperformed all TF-domain methods. From our research, this performance gap comes from three critical factors.

First, some attempts have been made [16,8] to model amplitude and phase separately, but no TF-domain AVSS method explores modelling the two acoustic dimensions (time and frequency) independently and in a tailored way, to exploit the advantage this domain has over T-domain methods. In fact, recent research in the AOSS domain by [17] and [18] has capitalized on this advantage and outperformed the T-domain counterparts by large margins. But they use large LSTM [19] and transformer [20] architectures, which is a heavy computational burden, so they are not an attractive solution for AVSS. Second, existing AVSS studies [9,12] have explored various strategies for audio-visual fusion, but they neglect to use visual features from multiple receptive fields to increase performance. This kind of visual information is important ā priōrī knowledge, and it is crucial for extracting the voice of the target speaker accurately. Third, TF-domain AVSS studies [16,8,7] often overlook that the features are complex underneath, and so they lose critical amplitude and phase information when they extract the target speaker's voice from the audio mixture. This makes the reconstruction of the inverse STFT (iSTFT) worse and leads to poorer performance of the model.

- 1. Our RTFS Blocks deal with the first issue by projecting the features to a compressed subspace. In this subspace we explicitly model both acoustic dimensions individually and then in tandem, and after that we apply an attentional mechanism (TF-AR) to restore the dimensions with minimal information loss. This lets us get the benefits of independent time-frequency processing without a substantial computational cost.

- 2. Our Cross-dimensional Attention Fusion (CAF) Block is a low parameter, computationally efficient solution to the second issue. It aggregates the multi-modal information with a multi-head attention strategy so that the visual cues of the target speaker are fused optimally into the audio features, which helps high quality separation.

- 3. Our Spectral Source Separation (S^{3}) Block deals with the third issue by explicitly reconstructing the plural features of the target speaker, so separation quality is higher and computational cost does not increase.

As far as we know, RTFS-Net is the first TF-domain AVSS method that outperforms all contemporary T-domain methods, and it does this while also having a clear advantage, reducing computational complexity by 83% and the parameter count by 90%. We also provide a Web page where sample results can be listened to, and our code will be open-sourced after publication for reproducibility.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
The ‘cocktail party problem’ [1,2,3] describes our ability to focus on a single speaker’s voice amidst numerous overlapping voices in a noisy environment. While humans tackle this problem effortlessly, replicating this ability in machines remains a longstanding challenge in the field of signal-processing. Audio-only Speech Separation (AOSS) methods [4,5,6], which solely utilize the mixed-speaker audio signal, face limitations in scenarios with strong background noise, reverberation, or heavy voice overlap. To overcome these issues, researchers turned to a multi-modal approach: Audio-visual Speech Separation (AVSS) [7,8,9]. AVSS methods integrate additional visual cues into the paradigm and can generally be split into two main classes: Time-domain (T-domain) and Time-Frequency domain (TF-domain) methods, each with their own benefits and challenges.

T-domain methods [10,9,11,12] work on the long, uncompressed and high-dimensional audio features returned by the 1D convolutional encoder design proposed by [13]. This approach facilitates fine-grained, high quality audio separation, but the high parameter count and computational complexity lead to extended training periods, intensive GPU usage and slow inference speeds. TF-domain methods [14,15,7], on the other hand, apply their algorithms to the complex 2D representation yielded by the Short-Time Fourier Transform (STFT). Typically, the STFT uses large windows and hop lengths to compress the data, resulting in more computationally efficient separation methods. However, historically, all TF-domain methods have been substantially outperformed by T-domain methods. Based on our research, this performance gap stems from three critical factors.

Firstly, while some attempts have been made [16,8] to model amplitude and phase separately, no TF-domain AVSS methods explore the independent and tailored modelling of the two acoustic dimensions (time and frequency) to exploit this domain’s advantage over T-domain methods. Indeed, recent research by [17] and [18] in the AOSS domain has capitalized on this advantage and outperformed T-domain counterparts by large margins. However, their use of large LSTM [19] and transformer [20] architectures leads to a heavy computational burden, making them an unattractive solution in the AVSS space. Secondly, while existing AVSS studies [9,12] have explored various audio-visual fusion strategies, they neglect using visual features from multiple receptive fields to increase model performance. This type of visual information serves as important ā priōrī knowledge, crucial for accurately extracting the target speaker’s voice. Thirdly, TF-domain AVSS studies [16,8,7] often overlook the underlying complex nature of the features, and hence lose critical amplitude and phase information when extracting the target speaker’s voice from the audio mixture. This degrades the reconstruction performance of the inverse STFT (iSTFT) and leads to poorer model performance.

In this work, we propose a novel TF-domain AVSS method, the Recursive Time-Frequency Separation Network (RTFS-Net, Figure 1), which provides a computationally efficient solution to the cocktail party problem using an STFT based audio encoder, a high-fidelity pretrained video encoder and a series of recursive RTFS Blocks to perform target speaker extraction. Our contributions are threefold:

- 1. Our RTFS Blocks tackle the first issue by projecting the features to a compressed subspace. There, we explicitly model both acoustic dimensions individually, then in tandem, before applying an attentional mechanism (TF-AR) to restore the dimensions with minimal information loss. This allows us to reap the benefits of independent time-frequency processing without bearing a substantial computational cost.

- 2. Our Cross-dimensional Attention Fusion (CAF) Block provides a low parameter, computationally efficient solution to the second issue by aggregating the multi-modal information through a multi-head attention strategy, in order to optimally fuse the visual cues of the target speaker into the audio features and facilitate high quality separation.

- 3. Our Spectral Source Separation (S^{3}) Block addresses the third issue by explicitly reconstructing the plural features of the target speaker, achieving higher quality separation without increasing computational cost.

We conducted comprehensive experimental evaluations on three widely used datasets: LRS2 [14], LRS3 [21] and VoxCeleb2 [22], to demonstrate the value of each contribution. To the best of our knowledge, RTFS-Net is the first TF-domain AVSS method to outperform all contemporary T-domain methods, and it achieves this while exhibiting a clear advantage, reducing computational complexity by 83% and the parameter count by 90%. We additionally provide a Web page where sample results can be listened to, and our code will be open-sourced after publication for reproducibility purposes.
